S01.text: Bondi Beach. On the fourteenth of December, twenty twenty-five, the first night of Hanukkah, it became the scene of the deadliest terror attack ever carried out on Australian soil. Fifteen people were killed.

S02.text: Afterwards, the whole country asked the same question. How did this happen here? Police say the gunmen were inspired by Islamic State. But the Australia they struck had been under strain for two years, ever since the war in Gaza began in October twenty twenty-three.

S03.text: This film follows the threads of that strain. Some go back seventy-eight years. One goes back just fourteen months, to a fire in Bondi.

S04.text: October, twenty twenty-four. In the early hours, a small kosher restaurant in Bondi goes up in flames. Nobody is hurt. Police treat it as a local crime. Seven weeks later, about seven hundred kilometres south-west, a synagogue in Melbourne is firebombed before dawn.

S05.text: What almost nobody knew then was that some of the people who lit these fires were allegedly paid. And, according to ASIO, the trail led to a government on the other side of the world.

S06.text: And on the night of the attack, one man ran toward the gunfire. His story became one of the most shared in the country. We'll come back to him.

S07.text: None of these threads explains Bondi on its own. But together, they show the country it happened in. And to understand that country, we have to follow the money first.

S08.text: For months, the fires looked like local crime. But Australia's domestic spy agency, ASIO, kept investigating. What its investigators found, ASIO's chief described as a layer cake of cut-outs.

S09.text: Middlemen overseas. Coordinators. And at the bottom, people in Australia, allegedly paid to do a job, not to make a point. Analysts call it crime as a service. It's deniable. And it's very hard to detect.

S10.text: August, twenty twenty-five. The Prime Minister announces ASIO's assessment. According to ASIO, Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps directed at least two of the attacks. The Bondi restaurant fire, and the Melbourne synagogue. He called them, quote, extraordinary and dangerous acts of aggression orchestrated by a foreign nation on Australian soil.

S11.text: Australia expelled Iran's ambassador. The first since the Second World War, the government said. Iran denied any involvement. In Parliament, then Opposition Leader Sussan Ley said the attacks aimed to, quote, turn neighbour against neighbour and Australian against Australian. Remember those words.

S12.text: That was one hundred and ten days before Bondi. But why would anyone use a fire in Bondi as a weapon at all? To answer that, we have to go back to a vote Australia cast first.

S13.text: November, nineteen forty-seven. The new United Nations votes on a plan to divide Palestine into a Jewish state and an Arab state. The committee behind it is chaired by Australia's foreign minister. And the first country to vote yes is Australia.

S14.text: Thirty years earlier, Australian Light Horsemen had charged at Beersheba, helping open the road to Jerusalem. So Australians shaped this land twice. Once on horseback. And once at a ballot.

S15.text: For many Jewish people, that vote is remembered as a rescue, after the Holocaust. For Palestinians, what followed in nineteen forty-eight is remembered as the Nakba. The catastrophe. When more than seven hundred thousand people fled or were expelled from their homes. The same event. Remembered in two opposite ways.

S16.text: Both memories sailed to Australia. Melbourne became home to one of the largest communities of Holocaust survivors outside Israel. Palestinian, Lebanese and other Arab families settled in Sydney's south-west. Today, about one hundred thousand Jewish Australians, and more than eight hundred thousand Muslim Australians, call this country home.

S17.text: So when war comes to the Middle East, it doesn't stay there. It arrives in Australian homes, as family. And in the two years before Bondi, it arrived in Canberra too.

S18.text: First, a choice almost nobody noticed. Dozens of Australian companies make parts for the F thirty-five fighter jet, and those parts go into a shared global pool. Australia's air force flies the F thirty-five. So does Israel's.

S19.text: Critics, including human rights groups and the Greens, say that makes Australia part of the war. The government says Australia has not supplied weapons to Israel since the war began, and that the parts are a separate matter that would not change what Israel can do.

S20.text: Then, a choice everyone noticed. In August twenty twenty-five, the Prime Minister announced Australia would recognise the State of Palestine. He called a two-state solution, quote, humanity's best hope to break the cycle of violence. And he reminded the country that Australia had been the first to back the U.N. plan, back in nineteen forty-seven.

S21.text: It was made official at the United Nations in September, with conditions. No role for Hamas, demilitarisation, and Palestinian elections. And it was attacked from both directions. The Coalition, Israel's government and many Jewish groups said it rewarded Hamas. A pro-Palestinian advocacy group called it, quote, completely meaningless, while Australia still traded with Israel.

S22.text: Then it turned personal. Israel's prime minister posted that history would remember Albanese as, quote, a weak politician who betrayed Israel and abandoned Australia's Jews. Albanese replied, quote, I don't take these things personally.

S23.text: Visas were cancelled on both sides. Relations between two old friends sank to their lowest point in decades. Abroad, Canberra was making choices. But for some Australian families, the war had already come much closer.

S24.text: Zomi Frankcom grew up in Sydney. She spent years feeding people in disaster zones. On the first of April, twenty twenty-four, she and six colleagues from World Central Kitchen were killed, when Israeli drone strikes hit what the charity called their clearly marked convoy in Gaza.

S25.text: Prime Minister Albanese called it, quote, completely unacceptable. Israel's prime minister said his forces had, quote, unintentionally harmed non-combatants. Her family said she would leave, quote, a legacy of compassion, bravery and love.

S26.text: A former Defence Force chief reviewed Israel's investigation for Australia. He found serious failures, but no evidence the convoy had been knowingly targeted. In twenty twenty-six, Israel's military decided not to press criminal charges. Her family called it an insult to her memory.

S27.text: An Australian grandmother was also among those killed in Israel. And Australian-Palestinians lost relatives in Gaza. Australia granted thousands of visitor visas to people fleeing Gaza. Supporters called it basic humanity. The opposition said vetting was rushed. The government said every applicant was checked.

S28.text: For these families, the war was never far away. And at home, it was pulling the country in two.

S29.text: It began on the seventh of October, twenty twenty-three. Hamas-led fighters crossed from Gaza into southern Israel. Around twelve hundred people were killed, most of them civilians, and around two hundred and fifty were taken hostage.

S30.text: It was the deadliest day for Jewish people since the Holocaust. Israel's military campaign in Gaza lasted two years. Gaza's Health Ministry, run by Hamas, reported tens of thousands of Palestinians killed. U.N. agencies broadly treat those figures as reliable, and Israel long disputed them. U.N. backed experts declared famine in parts of the territory.

S31.text: Back home, two days after October the seventh, the Opera House sails were lit in Israel's colours. That night, a pro-Palestinian rally gathered below. Flares were lit, and antisemitic chanting caused national outrage, though a later police review disputed exactly what was said.

S32.text: The fight moved onto phones and into courtrooms. The private details of hundreds of Jewish writers and artists were published online, and Parliament made malicious doxxing a crime. An ABC presenter was taken off air after sharing a human rights report on Gaza, and the Federal Court later found she'd been unlawfully sacked. Two cases. Opposite sides.

S33.text: Tens of thousands marched across the Harbour Bridge in the rain. Jewish groups recorded record numbers of antisemitic incidents. Muslim Australians, especially women wearing the hijab, reported record abuse. The government appointed two special envoys, one to combat antisemitism, and one to combat Islamophobia.

S34.text: Now look back. The fires. The jet parts. The expelled ambassador. The recognition. The court cases. The visas. All of it, in the two years before Bondi.

S35.text: In October twenty twenty-five, a U.S.-brokered ceasefire brought the surviving hostages home. Many hoped the worst was over. Sixty-five days after the ceasefire, it wasn't.

S36.text: Remember the fire, fourteen months earlier, in Bondi? Hanukkah is the festival of lights. On its first night, around a thousand people gathered by the beach to celebrate.

S37.text: Two gunmen, a father and son, opened fire. Police shot the father dead. His son was arrested. Fifteen people were killed. Among them, a ten-year-old girl, a retired police officer, a rabbi, and a Holocaust survivor.

S38.text: That night, the Prime Minister said, quote, an attack on Jewish Australians is an attack on every Australian.

S39.text: And in the middle of the horror, one man crouched behind a parked car, waited, and ran at one of the gunmen. He wrestled the gun away. He was shot and wounded.

S40.text: His name is Ahmed al Ahmed. A Syrian-born Muslim. A father of two. The attack was aimed at Jewish Australians. And one of the people who stood in its way was a Muslim Australian.

S41.text: The Prime Minister called his bravery, quote, an inspiration for all Australians. Police say the gunmen were inspired by Islamic State. And some warn that seeing Bondi only through Israel and Gaza risks missing the extremism behind it, or blaming whole communities for the acts of two men.

S42.text: Twenty-five days after the attack, the government called a Royal Commission on Antisemitism and Social Cohesion, led by a former High Court judge. In February, Israel's President visited Australia to comfort grieving families. In April, the commission called for tougher national gun laws. Its final report is due on the eighteenth of December, twenty twenty-six. Four days after the anniversary.

S43.text: So, what does a war fourteen thousand kilometres away have to do with Bondi? It didn't pull the trigger. But for two years, it pulled at the country. A vote Australia cast first. Parts in a fighter jet. Fires, ASIO says, directed from abroad.

S44.text: An ambassador expelled. A recognition. Australians grieving on both sides. ASIO says a foreign state tried to turn neighbour against neighbour. On a beach in Bondi, one neighbour ran toward the danger, for another.

S45.text: Maybe the real question isn't about the Middle East at all. It's whether a country built by people from everywhere can hold two communities' grief at the same time, without asking either to give up theirs. What Australia does next will say less about Gaza, and more about us.

S46.text: Is this Australia's issue? Tell us what you think. And if any of this has been hard to watch, you're not alone. Support details are in the description.
